newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow plans issue of $5 bln in bonds by mid-1998.
newsitem.headline: Moscow plans issue of $5 bln in bonds by mid-1998.

text.p: Moscow city authorities plan to issue three types of bonds totalling some $5 billion by mid-1998 to finance investment projects in the Russian capital, a senior official said on Tuesday.
Mechislav Klimovich, chairman of the city's securities committee, told a conference Moscow planned to issue discount bonds, similar to Treasury bills, savings bonds and Eurobonds.
Klimovich gave no breakdown of how much each issue would be worth but said all the proceeds would go to investment projects.
Moscow officials said last month the city was planning to issue foreign currency bonds, probably for $300 million, on international markets later this year.

Klimovich told Reuters details of the Euroloan were still being worked out. "The consultations are still under way, the tender is not yet complete. We are still waiting for several documents from our partners," he said.
He told the conference, organised by Euromoney magazine, Moscow spent about a third of its budget on construction. It was the financial centre of Russia but lacked the appropriate infrastructure.
Moscow, celebrating its 850th birthday next year, is a relative late-comer to Russia's municipal bond market.
St Petersburg, Russia's second city, has been issuing munis since March 1995 and has attracted international investors.

"We have a municipal bond market in Russia and in St Petersburg, in particular, more liquid than anything that exists in Eastern Europe at the moment," George Nianias, managing director of Denholm Hall, which has been the main foreign consultant to St Petersburg's municipal bond programme, said.

Igor Kostikov, director of the AVK investment firm which is general agent for the St Petersburg bonds, told the conference the city had made 50 issues. Of that, 15 were new tranches of earlier issues with a total value of 5.57 trillion roubles.
The maturity of the rouble-denominated paper is between three and 18 months. Kostikov said the city would like to make the loan longer term as interest rates fell.
St Petersburg mandated Salomon Brothers earlier this year to sell up to $200 million of paper to foreign investors.
Terms of the international issue have not been revealed.

But critics of the programme said St Petersburg city authorities have encountered budgetary problems, and there has been speculation the bond issues have come to resemble a pyramid scheme -- a charge also levelled regularly at the federal government's GKO Treasury bills.

However, Andrew Dobson, who is acting as a consultant on a number of Russian projects, including the St Petersburg municipal bond programme, for the British government's Know-How Fund, said it was not a pyramid scheme.
"You make sure that you do not borrow to pay your debt servicing costs and that has been part of St Petersburg's programme since it started," he told Reuters.
Dobson said as yields on T-bills fall, more authorities were likely to issue muncipal bonds, and if they could manage the foreign exchange costs, issue them on foreign markets.
"If GKO yields come down, a lot more people will find it a sensible thing to do," he said.
An issue of six-month St Petersburg munis yielded an average 58.09 percent on August 28 after 61.32 percent on an issue on August 14.
The Russian Federation is also planning an issue of Eurobonds but terms have yet to be fixed.
